title: Finite differences for heat and Laplace equations
subtitle: Replace derivatives by differences on a grid and a partial differential equation becomes arithmetic.

sections.title: Kinds of PDE
sections.body:
Partial differential equations come in three personalities, and knowing which one you have decides how you solve it. Second-order linear PDEs Auₓₓ + Buₓᵧ + Cuᵧᵧ = … are elliptic (B² − 4AC < 0: Laplace, Poisson, steady states), parabolic (= 0: the heat equation, diffusion) or hyperbolic (> 0: the wave equation, propagation).

The type decides which numerical scheme is stable and what boundary or initial data are needed. Classify uₜ = α uₓₓ: write it as α uₓₓ − uₜ = 0, with only one second derivative (A = α, B = C = 0), so B² − 4AC = 0. The 1-D heat equation is parabolic.

worked.why: Classify uₜ = α uₓₓ: write it as α uₓₓ − uₜ = 0, with only one second derivative (A = α, B = C = 0).

keynotes: Second-order linear PDEs are elliptic (B² − 4AC < 0: Laplace, Poisson), parabolic (= 0: heat equation) or hyperbolic (> 0: wave equation).
The type decides which numerical scheme is stable and what boundary or initial data are needed.
The 1-D heat equation uₜ = α uₓₓ has A = α and B = C = 0, so B² − 4AC = 0: parabolic.

sections.title: Finite-difference approximations
sections.body:
How do you teach a computer calculus? You replace each derivative by a difference between neighbouring grid values. Central differences on a grid with spacing h: uₓ ≈ (uᵢ₊₁ − uᵢ₋₁)/(2h), uₓₓ ≈ (uᵢ₊₁ − 2uᵢ + uᵢ₋₁)/h². In time, uₜ ≈ (uᵢⁿ⁺¹ − uᵢⁿ)/Δt. Each approximation has a known truncation error.

Test the second difference on u = x² at x = 2 with h = 0.5: u(1.5) = 2.25, u(2) = 4, u(2.5) = 6.25. Then uₓₓ ≈ (2.25 − 8 + 6.25)/0.25 = 2, which is exact. The central second-difference of a parabola is exact.

questions.prompt: The central second-difference of a parabola is…

choices.text: Exact — the formula is exact for quadratics.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The error term involves the fourth derivative.

keynotes: Central differences on a grid with spacing h: uₓ ≈ (uᵢ₊₁ − uᵢ₋₁)/(2h) and uₓₓ ≈ (uᵢ₊₁ − 2uᵢ + uᵢ₋₁)/h².
For u = x² at x = 2 with h = 0.5 the second difference is (2.25 − 8 + 6.25)/0.25 = 2, exact.

sections.title: The explicit scheme for the heat equation
sections.body:
Now you can watch heat flow along a metal rod, one time step at a time. The explicit scheme is uᵢⁿ⁺¹ = uᵢⁿ + r(uᵢ₋₁ⁿ − 2uᵢⁿ + uᵢ₊₁ⁿ), r = αΔt/Δx². Each new value is a weighted average of a point and its neighbours. A rod with ends at 100 and 0 starts at 0 and relaxes toward the straight line: after 400 steps the middle reads 49.997 (steady value 50).

Try one node: neighbours 100 and 0, itself at 0, r = 0.25. New value = 0 + 0.25(100 − 0 + 0) = 25. The scheme is stable only if r ≤ ½. If r exceeds 0.5, the numbers oscillate and blow up. The successive profiles in the figure show the heat diffusing along the rod.

worked.why: Interior node with neighbours 100 and 0, itself at 0, r = 0.25.

questions.prompt: What happens if r > 0.5 in the explicit scheme?

choices.text: The numerical solution oscillates and grows without bound.

figures.caption: Figure 6.3.1 — heat diffusing along a rod
figures.note: Successive profiles; dark curves are earlier times.

problems.prompt: Why does the simulator refuse r = 0.6? What can you change?
problems.answer: The explicit scheme is stable only for αΔt/Δx² ≤ ½. Reduce the time step Δt (or increase Δx) until r ≤ 0.5.

keynotes: In the explicit scheme each new value is a weighted average of a point and its neighbours, with r = αΔt/Δx².
A rod with ends at 100 and 0 relaxes towards the straight line: after 400 steps the middle reads 49.997 (steady value 50).
The scheme is stable only if r ≤ ½.

sections.title: Laplace’s equation: relaxation
sections.body:
When nothing changes in time any more, as you will find, the heat equation becomes Laplace’s equation, and it has a very friendly numerical meaning: every interior value is the average of its four neighbours. ∇²u = 0 becomes uᵢⱼ = ¼(uᵢ₊₁,ⱼ + uᵢ₋₁,ⱼ + uᵢ,ⱼ₊₁ + uᵢ,ⱼ₋₁).

Start with a guess, set the boundary values, and repeatedly replace each point by the average (Gauss–Seidel iteration) until nothing changes. This is exactly the electrostatic potential in a box with fixed-voltage walls. Try a 3×3 grid with the top edge 100 and other edges 0: for the single interior point, u = ¼(100 + 0 + 0 + 0) = 25. At a solution of Laplace’s equation each interior point equals the average of its four neighbours.

worked.why: A 3×3 grid, top edge 100, other edges 0. Find the centre value by symmetry with all four neighbours averaging in.
For the single interior point: u = ¼(100 + 0 + 0 + 0).

questions.prompt: At a solution of Laplace’s equation each interior point equals…

keynotes: Laplace’s equation ∇²u = 0 becomes uᵢⱼ = ¼(uᵢ₊₁,ⱼ + uᵢ₋₁,ⱼ + uᵢ,ⱼ₊₁ + uᵢ,ⱼ₋₁): every interior value is the average of its four neighbours.
Start with a guess, set the boundary values and repeatedly average (Gauss–Seidel iteration) until nothing changes; this is the electrostatic potential in a box with fixed-voltage walls.
For a 3×3 grid with the top edge 100 and other edges 0, the single interior point is ¼(100 + 0 + 0 + 0) = 25.

sections.title: Implicit schemes and accuracy
sections.body: The explicit scheme has a leash: r ≤ ½ ties your time step to the grid. Can you cut it? The implicit (backward-time) scheme and Crank–Nicolson evaluate the spatial differences at the new time level. Each step solves a tridiagonal linear system (Gaussian elimination in O(n)), but they are stable for any step size, so you can choose the time step for accuracy only. Crank–Nicolson is second-order in time. Implicit schemes are attractive because they stay stable at large time steps.

questions.prompt: Implicit schemes are attractive because they…

choices.text: Remain stable for large time steps, at the cost of solving a system each step.

keynotes: The implicit (backward-time) scheme and Crank–Nicolson evaluate the spatial differences at the new time level.
Each step solves a tridiagonal linear system (Gaussian elimination in O(n)), but they are stable for any step size.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
Two lines to remember.

  • Central differences turn PDEs into arithmetic on a grid.
  • Explicit heat scheme needs r ≤ ½; Laplace relaxes to the neighbour average.
keynotes: Central differences turn PDEs into arithmetic on a grid.
The explicit heat scheme needs r ≤ ½ and Laplace relaxes to the neighbour average.
